rv.q: Until stymied by an overlong second act, pushing the evening close to three hours, the cast achieves the speed farce needs.
Tartuffe (Remixed) works for a number of reasons: it honours the beats and intentions of the original play, but reinvents them in a vibrant new way.
Overall then, a refresh which speaks to multiculturalism, loyalty, traditions, and in a world which daily gives us cause to question established truth, a healthy and appropriate dose of cynicism.
Raymond's 'remix' proves an entertaining and occasionally touching farce in spite of, rather than due to, Mark Rylance's overstated performance as the central character.
While the project is flawed, she and Rylance make this worth seeing.
Tartuffe (Remixed) is a vibrant and riotous comedy with a starkly dark undertone.

Transposing the narrative into an African-Caribbean household is a masterstroke. Adherence to religious values and the importance of Pentecostal or Charismatic church communities is a colonial throwback and still features large within the African diaspora.
Tartuffe (Remixed) is energetic, clever and hilarious, while still finding room to explore family, faith and tradition. Go and see it if you haven't already.
Darren Raymond expands his scale: both as writer and director with his Intermission Theatre, in this fizzing, rich verse-adaptation of Moliere's 1664 play.
The adaptation is genuinely inspired and manages to breathe fresh life into a story that is more than 350 years old.
A riotous night out is to be had here, whether you know the original text or not.

cn.t: Raymond's vibrant update relocates Molière's classic to a Nigerian-Jamaican family with clever rhyming couplets and Rylance's grotesque conman at its center. Critics praise the fizzing adaptation's relevance and humor, though some find it loses political edge.
